newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Funds drive sell-off in commodities.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Funds drive sell-off in commodities.

text.p: Commodity markets stood jolted at week's end by a sell-off led by the speculative funds that seemed to reflect the unease about interest rates that had earlier hit Wall Street

"This was the day for the funds to get out of everything that smacked of positive economic growth," said brokerage GNI Ltd, commenting on how the selling hit silver and the industrial metals late on Thursday. Several markets were again under pressure on Friday.
Coffee was a spectacular victim. A mass bale-out there followed a rally that had taken coffee futures up 50 percent since January.

Although some buying was seen on cocoa, and crude oil seemed steadier on Friday after a big slide, it does not look yet as if much "hot" money coming out of other assets is finding a home in commodities.
In the latest volatility, Friday saw London May Robusta coffee bean futures drop five percent after an even bigger Thursday fall - of about eight percent - in New York on the premium Arabica types.
Traders said that word of rising US coffee stocks took the heat from a speculative fever that was fuelled by earlier concern about tight Latin American supply.
In February, coffee stocks rose 204,000 132-pound bags to 1,546,000 bags, according to the Green Coffee Association of New York.
"Funds are massively long in coffee," said a London trader. "They may be looking for another good fund performer like cocoa. Cocoa is a good candidate for funds after the recent run-up."
But he added that "if the prices come in much lower, the specs may start to re-position themselves again ahead of the Brazilian frost season in June and July."
Copper, aluminium and zinc prices have tumbled, also on selling mostly out of the United States by the funds.
"No doubt the disruption of the US stock markets and concern about interest rates is making them look at their portfolio," said a senior metals trader.

The flagship three-months copper price ended 1996 on the London Metal Exchange at $2,127 per tonne. It got to $2,440 on March 7 but it closed down at $2,336 on Friday after a drop of more than $50 in the last 24 hours.
Also on the LME, fund selling hit nickel on Friday sending it lower by $160 to $7,470.

GNI says the funds and consumer stock building fuelled the rally in metals during the first quarter of the year. Unless there is a strong pick-up in the global economy, it says, a decline is now most likely.
"If the consumer stockbuilding was done in Q1 and the funds are long there is only one way for the metals to go in Q2," it says.

Continued fund selling of silver in New York on Thursday pressured precious metals. London gold closed at $347.45 on Friday after being around $350 at mid-weekwhilst silver is at its lowest since mid-January at around $4.70 per ounce.
Crude oil prices were somewhat steadier on Friday with the benchmark North Sea Brent Blend around $18.25 per barrel on the May contract after a slide of about $1 to nine-month lows mid-week.
Funds joined a sell-off in oil that was otherwise based on views that more Iraqi supply is coming to the market at the time of the cyclical second quarter weakness in demand.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, grain and soybean prices have fallen sharply after latest weekly US export shipments came in below the estimates of most analysts and crop weather in America improved.
Wheat for May delivery has fallen some 15 cents since Wednesday to trade just above $3.70 per bushel at around the mid-session on Friday.
May soybeans fell extended a slide to open Friday sharply lower at $8.64 per bushel.
